name: Hirsutism
aliases: excessive terminal hair growth in women

clinicalPearls: Hirsutism is defined as excessive growth of terminal (long, coarse, pigmented) hair in an androgen-dependent distribution and affects roughly 10% of reproductive-age women (Harrison 22e p.3137).
Most cases are idiopathic or due to androgen excess from polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS); PCOS is the single most common cause of ovarian androgen excess (Harrison 22e p.3137-3140).

Hirsutism must be distinguished from hypertrichosis, which is androgen-independent generalized excess vellus/terminal hair often caused by medications such as phenytoin, minoxidil, and cyclosporine (Harrison 22e p.3138).

Virilization (deepened voice, breast atrophy, increased muscle bulk, clitoromegaly, increased libido) signals markedly elevated androgens and raises concern for an ovarian or adrenal neoplasm, or hyperthecosis (Harrison 22e p.3138).
Sudden onset and rapid progression of hirsutism, especially with virilization, suggests an androgen-secreting tumor and warrants urgent evaluation (Harrison 22e p.3138).

The modified Ferriman-Gallwey scale grades nine androgen-sensitive sites from 0 to 4; a normal score is <8, and scores >=8 in most non-Hispanic white and African American women indicate excess androgen-mediated hair growth (Harrison 22e p.3138-3139).
Asian and Native American women are less likely to manifest hirsutism even with androgen excess; pustular acne and scalp hair thinning may be the only cutaneous clues (Harrison 22e p.3138).

Free (unbound) testosterone is often more informative than total testosterone, because hyperinsulinemia and androgen excess lower SHBG, keeping total testosterone high-normal while unbound testosterone is substantially elevated (Harrison 22e p.3139-3140).

Dihydrotestosterone (DHT), formed from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase within the pilosebaceous unit, is the principal mediator of androgen action on the hair follicle; type 2 isoenzyme predominates in hair follicles and type 1 in sebaceous glands (Harrison 22e p.3139).
Acanthosis nigricans and skin tags are cutaneous markers of associated insulin resistance in hyperandrogenic women (Harrison 22e p.3138).
A BMI >25 kg/m2 (and especially >30) is frequently associated with hirsutism, partly via increased peripheral conversion of androgen precursors to testosterone (Harrison 22e p.3138).

After menopause, ovarian estrogen production falls more than androgen production and SHBG declines, increasing the relative proportion of unbound testosterone, which can exacerbate hirsutism (Harrison 22e p.3140).
harrison.pathophysiology: Androgens drive differentiation of pilosebaceous units, transforming vellus hairs into terminal hairs and stimulating sebaceous gland development; the total number of follicles is fixed for life, but follicle size and hair type change with androgen exposure and local growth factors. Testosterone, secreted roughly equally by ovaries (LH-driven) and adrenals (ACTH-driven), is a precursor that is converted within the pilosebaceous unit by 5-alpha-reductase to the more potent dihydrotestosterone, the chief local mediator. End-organ sensitivity, genetic and ethnic background, and local growth factors explain why androgen levels correlate only modestly with the amount of hair. Excess androgen also shortens the scalp-hair anagen phase, producing thinning/androgenic alopecia. Hyperinsulinemia and androgen excess suppress hepatic SHBG, raising bioavailable free testosterone. In nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (usually 21-hydroxylase deficiency), impaired cortisol synthesis reduces negative feedback, driving compensatory ACTH-mediated adrenal hyperplasia and accumulation of steroid precursors that are shunted to androgens (Harrison 22e p.3138-3141).
additionalDifferentials: Polycystic ovary syndrome / functional ovarian hyperandrogenism
Nonclassic and classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (most often 21-hydroxylase deficiency)
Pregnancy-related hyperandrogenism (hyperreactio luteinalis, thecoma of pregnancy)
Drug-induced (androgens, androgenic progestins, minoxidil, phenytoin, diazoxide, cyclosporine, valproic acid)
nonInfectiousMimics: Hypertrichosis (androgen-independent generalized hair growth, often drug-induced)
Constitutional/ethnic variation in hair distribution mistaken for pathologic hirsutism
additionalInvestigations: Total testosterone (specialty assay) and free/unbound testosterone, calculated from total testosterone and SHBG or measured by LC/tandem mass spectrometry
DHEAS to assess adrenal androgen contribution
Morning follicular-phase 17-hydroxyprogesterone to screen for 21-hydroxylase deficiency; ACTH (cosyntropin) stimulation test if equivocal
Dexamethasone androgen-suppression test to broadly distinguish adrenal from ovarian androgen overproduction
Overnight 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test with 8 a.m. cortisol when Cushing's syndrome is suspected
Prolactin and thyroid function when galactorrhea or other features present
CT or MRI to localize a suspected adrenal mass; transvaginal ultrasound for a suspected ovarian mass
Note: LH/FSH and ovarian ultrasound have limited diagnostic value for PCOS given pulsatile gonadotropin secretion and low ultrasound specificity
redFlags: Rapid onset or rapid progression of hirsutism
Signs of virilization: voice deepening, clitoromegaly, breast atrophy, increased muscle bulk
Total testosterone >12 nmol/L (>3.5 ng/mL) suggesting an androgen-producing tumor
DHEAS >18.5 micromol/L (>7000 microg/L) suggesting an adrenal tumor
Hypertension, striae, easy bruising, centripetal weight gain suggesting Cushing's syndrome
harrison.prognosis: Most hirsutism is benign and chronic, reflecting underlying functional androgen excess (commonly PCOS) or idiopathic causes; with treatment, hair growth typically progresses slowly. Even effective therapy yields only modest reduction in hair, with attenuation usually not evident until 4-6 months and maximal effect requiring 9-12 months because of the length of the hair growth cycle. By contrast, rapidly progressive hirsutism with virilization may herald a malignant or otherwise serious neoplasm and carries a prognosis tied to that underlying tumor (Harrison 22e p.3138-3141).
pitfalls: Relying on total testosterone alone can miss hyperandrogenism, since low SHBG can keep total levels high-normal while free testosterone is elevated.
Assuming shaving increases hair rate or density; it does not.

Over-interpreting ovarian ultrasound: polycystic-appearing ovaries also occur in hypothalamic amenorrhea and in women without PCOS, so ultrasound has low specificity and is often unnecessary to diagnose PCOS.
Random LH/FSH measurements are unreliable for PCOS because of pulsatile gonadotropin secretion.
Mild DHEAS elevations are common in PCOS and do not by themselves indicate an adrenal tumor.
Failing to distinguish hirsutism from hypertrichosis, leading to inappropriate hormonal work-up.
Underestimating androgen excess in Asian and Native American women, who may show only acne or scalp thinning.
harrison.severityClassification: Hair growth is quantified objectively with the modified Ferriman-Gallwey scale, scoring nine androgen-sensitive body sites from 0 (no terminal hair) to 4 (frankly virile, male-pattern). A total score <8 is normal in ~95% of non-Hispanic white and African American women; scores >=8 indicate excess androgen-mediated hair growth warranting hormonal evaluation (Harrison 22e p.3138-3139).
management: Treat the underlying cause, particularly weight reduction and metabolic optimisation in polycystic ovary syndrome
Androgen suppression with a combined oral contraceptive as first-line pharmacotherapy
Anti-androgen therapy such as spironolactone, cyproterone acetate or finasteride
Topical eflornithine to slow facial terminal-hair growth alongside mechanical hair removal by laser or electrolysis
Insulin sensitiser such as metformin where insulin resistance accompanies polycystic ovary syndrome
Glucocorticoid therapy where non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the cause
Urgent endocrine referral and tumour resection where virilisation or rapid onset suggests an androgen-secreting neoplasm, counselling on the slow, months-long treatment response
